patch.description_long: Bonwit Teller’s Fifth Avenue building contained two large Art Deco limestone reliefs and a decorative metal grille. In 1980, as the site was cleared for Trump Tower, Donald Trump agreed that the sculptures would be removed and donated to the Metropolitan Museum of Art. The museum had arranged to receive them, but contractors demolished the pieces with the building. Trump and project representatives cited the cost and delay involved in removing them; preservationists and museum officials criticized their loss. Accounts differ about who authorized the demolition and when that decision was made, so the episode is best described as the destruction of the works after a public donation commitment, without assigning a specific personal order. Trump Tower later opened on the site in 1983. The building’s redevelopment proceeded, and Trump Tower opened in 1983. The preservation dispute became a notable episode in New York’s debate over landmark buildings.

patch.description_long: President Donald Trump dismissed about 17 inspectors general across federal agencies late on January 24, 2025, including watchdogs at the Departments of Defense, State and Transportation. Inspectors general audit agency spending, investigate misconduct and report findings to agency leaders and Congress. A 2022 amendment to the Inspector General Act requires 30 days’ advance notice to Congress and a substantive rationale before a removal. The administration sent termination notices but had not provided that advance notice before the dismissals. Senate Judiciary Committee chair Chuck Grassley said the required detailed notice had not been supplied. The administration argued the president had authority to remove executive officials. The dismissals raised concerns about oversight and led to disputes over statutory compliance and presidential authority; the event does not establish that every individual removal was later ruled unlawful. Subsequent legal and congressional proceedings addressed different aspects of the dispute.
